title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E555 uses infinite Lagrange interpolation. The function f(z) = sin(zΦ)/z is known at the nodes z = a, b, c, ... (the 'sines of the arcs'). Interpolating it at z = 0 gives f(0) = Φ, so the arc Φ is recovered from the values sin(aΦ), sin(bΦ), .... Formula (7) of the paper is this Lagrange formula, Φ = Σ_k [sin(z_kΦ)/z_k]·Π_{j≠k} z_j/(z_j − z_k).

Example 3 (§25) takes an interleaved arithmetic progression of nodes: m, n, 1+m, 1+n, 2+m, 2+n, .... Euler says the general case gives nothing notable, then specialises to n = 1 − m. The nodes are then m, 1−m, 1+m, 2−m, 2+m, .... He writes
Φ = 𝔄 sin mΦ/m − 𝔅 sin(1−m)Φ/(1−m) + ℭ sin(1+m)Φ/(1+m) − ...
with the coefficients given as infinite products. From the shape of these products he reads off the ratios 𝔅/𝔄 = m/(1−m), ℭ/𝔅 = (1−m)/(1+m), and so on. Hence every coefficient equals m𝔄 divided by its own node, and he obtains
MΦ = Σ_{k∈Z} sin((k+m)Φ)/(k+m)², where M = 1/(m𝔄).
He identifies 𝔄 with a quotient of Beta integrals via an earlier 'reduction'. Differentiating in Φ gives
M = Σ_{k∈Z} cos((k+m)Φ)/(k+m).
Setting Φ = 0 gives M = 1/m − 1/(1−m) + 1/(1+m) − ... = π cot mπ, his old partial-fraction result. Equating this with the integral expression for M yields a Beta-integral identity. It is equivalent to
B(m+1,m)·B(m,1−m) = π cot(mπ)·B(m,1−2m),
which is true: it follows from Γ-reflection plus duplication. The next page reshapes it into B(m,m)·B(m,1−m) = 2π cot(mπ)·B(m,1−2m), which is Corollary 3.

Modern reading:
- Σ_k e^{ikφ}/(k+m) = π e^{im(π−φ)}/sin(mπ) for 0<φ<2π. So Σ_k cos((k+m)φ)/(k+m) = π cot mπ for |φ|<2π, and Σ sin((k+m)φ)/(k+m)² = π cot(mπ)·φ for |φ| ≤ 2π.
- For the even function sin(zΦ)/z, sampling at {k ± m} is a union of two shifted integer lattices (density 2). That is why the reconstruction works up to bandwidth 2π.
- Compare the uniform-lattice cardinal (Whittaker–Shannon) series Φ = (sin πm/π)·Σ(−1)^k sin((k+m)Φ)/(k+m)². It is valid only for |Φ| ≤ π.
errors: The cosine series is stated (here implicitly, and explicitly on p.180, 'angulum quemcunque') for arbitrary Φ. Σ cos((k+m)φ)/(k+m) = π cot mπ holds only for |φ| < 2π. For 2π < φ < 4π it equals π cos(3mπ)/sin(mπ), since the series is e^{imφ} times a 2π-periodic function. The same restriction (|φ| ≤ 2π) applies to the sine series MΦ = Σ sin((k+m)Φ)/(k+m)². Consequently the next page's specialisations φ = π/(2m) and φ = π/m are valid only for m > 1/4, respectively m ≥ 1/2.

As machine-transcribed, M = ∫x^m(1−x)^{m−1}·∫x^{m−1}(1−x)^{1−m}/∫x^{m−1}(1−x)^{−m} equals (1−m)B(m+1,m) = (1−m)Γ(m)²/(2Γ(2m)). This is not π cot mπ: at m = 1/2 it gives π/4, not 0. The version consistent with p.180 and Corollary 3 is M = ∫x^m(1−x)^{m−1}·∫x^{m−1}(1−x)^{−m}/∫x^{m−1}(1−x)^{−2m}, and this is correct. The discrepancy is most likely an OCR error, but it should be checked against the image.

Convergence of the infinite Lagrange products is not addressed. Taken in the natural order, Π_{j≠m} z_j/(z_j − m) = Π_k (k²−m²)/(k(k−2m)) diverges (factors ~ 1+2m/k). The value of 𝔄 therefore depends on how the factors are grouped. The final identity is nevertheless correct with M = π cot mπ.
The integral identity needs 0 < m < 1/2 for ∫x^{m−1}(1−x)^{−2m} to converge. This is not stated.

ideas.what: Recovering Φ from sin(zΦ) at infinitely many nodes by infinite Lagrange interpolation of sin(zΦ)/z at z = 0
ideas.modern_name: infinite Lagrange interpolation / sampling series for a band-limited (entire, exponential type) function
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cardinal series: E.T. Whittaker 1915, Kotelnikov 1933, Shannon 1949. Precursors: Cauchy, Borel
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opuscula Analytica I, 1783). Euler's interpolation theme also appears in E555's neighbours; no further specific reference known

ideas.what: Interpolation at the two-lattice node set {k+m}∪{k−m}, giving a weight-1/z_k sampling formula valid for bandwidth up to 2π for even functions
Σ_{k∈Z} cos((k+m)φ)/(k+m) = π cot mπ and Σ sin((k+m)φ)/(k+m)² = π φ cot mπ
ideas.modern_name: Fourier series of e^{imφ} on an interval; Lerch/Hurwitz-type periodic zeta at s=1,2
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Fourier series of cos mx); later Lerch
ideas.where_published: Closely related cos(mx) expansions occur in other Euler papers; exact reference unsure
Introductio in analysin infinitorum (E101), Ch. X

ideas.what: B(m+1,m)B(m,1−m) = π cot(mπ) B(m,1−2m), equivalently B(m,m)B(m,1−m) = 2π cot(mπ) B(m,1−2m)
ideas.modern_name: consequence of Γ reflection and duplication (Legendre) formulas
ideas.where_published: E555 §25–29; Euler's 'Observationes circa integralia formularum ∫x^{p−1}dx(1−x^n)^{q/n−1}' series of papers (E321 etc.) give similar relations

missed.claim: Euler's specialisation n = 1−m is effectively a periodic nonuniform sampling theorem. The even entire function sin(zΦ)/z is reconstructed from samples on the union of lattices {k+m} and {k−m}, with all weights proportional to 1/z_k. Applying the even-function symmetry, the reconstruction is valid on a band (|Φ|<2π) twice that of the single-lattice cardinal series. Histories of the sampling theorem do not, to my knowledge, cite E555's interleaved-node example as a precursor of recurrent/two-channel sampling.
missed.quote: Si arcus a, b, c, d, etc. constituant progressionem arithmeticam interruptam ... ex eorum finibus longitudinem arcus Φ definire
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical precursor for nonuniform sampling theory. It also shows Euler noticing the identity's validity is independent of Φ, though without seeing the 2π band limit.

deep.surprise_reason: The results themselves (π cot mπ partial fractions, Fourier-type series, the Beta identity) are Euler-known or routine consequences of Γ identities. The mildly notable aspect is the sampling-theoretic content of the interleaved-node interpolation, which is plausibly overlooked in sampling-theory histories.
transcription_corrections: The M definition and final comparison as transcribed give a false identity. Read consistently with p.180/Cor. 3: M = ∫x^m dx(1−x)^{m−1}·∫x^{m−1}dx(1−x)^{−m} / ∫x^{m−1}dx(1−x)^{−2m}, and ∫x^m dx(1−x)^{m−1} = (π cos mπ/sin mπ)·∫x^{m−1}dx(1−x)^{−2m} / ∫x^{m−1}dx(1−x)^{−m}. Correspondingly 𝔄 = ∫x^{m−1}dx(1−x)^{−2m} / (m∫x^m dx(1−x)^{m−1}·∫x^{m−1}dx(1−x)^{−m}). Verify against the image.

On the next page (p.180–181) the exponent 'n' in x^n, x^{n−1} should be m (x^m, x^{m−1}). The substitution m = λ/n, x = y^n in Corollary 3 confirms the first factor is x^{m−1}dx. With free n the stated identity is false (n = 1 is a counterexample).
The coefficient formulas from solution (7) are illegible in the transcription. They are Lagrange-type products Π z_j/(z_j − z_k) over the remaining nodes.
